newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen steady to firm at open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen steady to firm at open.

text.p: Wall Street shares are expected to open steady to firmer on Wednesday, amid a lower interest rate environment and growing optimism that a new government plan to cut taxes would benefit stocks long-term.

But analysts said markets would continue to scrutinize a stream of economic data due out this week, including June new home sales data due today at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT and the key July employment report, due on Friday.

"There is some residual benefit from the tax bill, given all the stories which have come out about how it will benefit stocks," Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said. "Plus bonds have been strong."
Stocks were still digesting news that late Monday, President Clinton and Congress negotiated tax cut proposals as part of an agreement to balance the federal budget.
Tax cuts were estimated to amount to more than $90 billion over five years. Among proposals are provisions for cuts in the capital gains tax rate.

"The optimism continues," Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co, said. "Stocks appear headed higher and bond yields look lower. The market liked the composition of the tax bill yesterday."

The Dow Jones Industrial average opened lower on Tuesday, after the second quarter employment cost index came in as forecast, without posting a positive surprise. But it reversed and staged a rally later, finishing up 53 points at 8175.
In early trading on Wednesday, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index rose 1.65 points to 948.60, while the long bond gained 13/32 to yield 6.36 percent.
But Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal, said stocks might open lower because Tuesday's gains were led by a narrow core of stocks.
"It leaves open the question of what comes next," he said.

Markets would pay some attention to new home sales for June, forecast to fall to 818,000 from 825,000 in May. But Friday's employment report, which has shaken financial markets in the past, remained the focus, analysts said.
"Bonds are waiting for the July employment report on Friday," Battipaglia said. "It could just be a watch-and-wait sort of day."

The dollar was off session highs against the yen in Tokyo after briefly rising on Japan's industrial output data for June. It was trading at 118.35/45 yen. In Europe, the dollar was firm, trading at 1.8421/26 marks.
Japan's Nikkei average closed off 189.92 points, or 0.93 percent, at 20,212.82.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 37.3 at 4913.9.
U.S. stocks were mixed to higher in London trading, boosted by yesterday's rally on Wall Street but cautious ahead of U.S. economic data.
The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that Wall Street analysts are debating whether the drop in Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp's share price has created a buying opportunity.

The New York Times said in its Market Place column that shares of Loehmann's Inc have fallen since around mid-April, when it warned of an earnings shorfall. Analysts say the problems come from changes in the apparel business and missteps by management.
